implementation_notes: The assignment statement evaluates the right-hand side (a tuple) first and then assigns it to the targets left to right, so `a, b = b, a` is the exchange itself - no temporary, no allocation of the represented state, and no way for the operation to fail, because Python has no user-defined assignment operators and objects are references. What replaces the C++ structure is "keep the representation behind one attribute and exchange the reference": `self._state, other._state = other._state, self._state` moves a whole object graph in one statement, and swapping the __dict__ of two plain instances moves both state dictionaries at once. The one place user code (and therefore an exception) enters is attribute or item assignment, which goes through __setattr__, descriptors, properties and __setitem__ - keep the exchanged members as plain attributes when the swap must not fail.
pitfalls: Attribute or item assignment runs user code (__setattr__, property setters, descriptors, __setitem__) which may raise or validate - a swap through them can fail after the first side was assigned; swap plain attributes or whole __dict__s instead.

`a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]` is safe even when i == j because the right-hand side is evaluated before any assignment, but two separate assignment statements are not - never write a swap as two statements.

Instances using __slots__ have no __dict__ to exchange, and swapping the dictionaries of instances with different attribute shapes leaves a broken object; keep the representation in one dedicated attribute.
The right-hand side allocates a tuple per swap (cheaper to use a temporary in inner loops), and releasing the old reference can trigger __del__ or weakref callbacks at the moment of the exchange.
